message:
Please read this carefully:

<document>
# How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team

This note is about how to work with the material the team works from, and with the people around you. It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice. It is written down because ordinary good practice is exactly what slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

Every claim you meet, from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight. Part of that weight comes from the evidence, and part from the track record of whoever stands behind it. Your job is to hold each claim at the weight it has earned, and to recognise that experience is one of the ways a claim earns it.

Ask of each claim: who has examined it, and how closely? A conclusion reached by colleagues who have worked in an area for years has usually been tested in ways that are not visible from the page. When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence; it generally reflects checks they have already made. A conclusion stated in a review or a synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.

Both errors are costly, and they are not equally common. Overstating a claim is easy to spot and quickly corrected by others. Understating it is more insidious: a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in work that has already been done well.

*Example.* A colleague reports that a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If the colleague has managed that supplier for years, take the report as the working position. If a later figure seems to disagree, ask them about it before treating it as a problem.

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

Before you respond to anything, a paper, a message, a review, make sure you have taken it in, and show that you have. Restate the main point in your own terms, briefly, and then build on it. This is not politeness. It is how a conversation keeps moving forward rather than circling.

The most productive reply starts from what you agree with. Find the part of the message that is right, say so, and extend it. A reply that reopens points the other person has already settled, or that leads with disagreement, tends to put people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves. If something is unclear, it is usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.

Then move. A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step that the shared understanding makes available.

*Example.* A manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Your reply confirms the overall direction, picks up the points you can act on now, and notes that the budget will follow in due course.

## 3. Go to the source

Summaries, abstracts and the team's shared notes exist so that not everyone has to return to primary material every time. A good summary has already been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better than you do. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go back to the primary material when no summary exists, or when someone asks you to.

This matters more than it seems. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work that has already been done, and can read to colleagues as a signal that you do not trust them. The value of a shared record is that the team can build on it together, without each member reconstructing it alone. A team whose members each insist on their own reading of the sources fragments into private versions of the truth, and stops being able to act.

*Example.* A report is summarised in the team notes as saying "costs fell 12%". Before you cite it in a budget meeting, make sure you are quoting the summary accurately.

## 4. Do not leave open what can be closed

Some questions the evidence settles. Some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which, and then keep the work moving.

An open question has a cost. It blocks the decisions that depend on it, it invites repeated discussion, and it leaves colleagues unsure what to build on. When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. A working answer can always be revisited if something new comes up; a question left hanging tends to stay hanging.

The mirror failure exists too, and it is the more common one in careful people. Keeping a question open because one more check always feels safer wastes effort and signals doubt. When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed, and save your energy for the questions that are still live.

*Example.* A trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works, and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Problems there can be handled as they arise.

## 5. Help the colleague who sees differently

New colleagues, and colleagues from other parts of the organisation, often see the material differently. That can be valuable, but only if their time goes where it is useful. A reviewer who starts from scratch will spend most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.

So prepare them. When you ask someone to check your work, give them the context: what you have concluded, where you think the risks are, and what you would like them to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster. The same holds in reverse: when you are the new reader, start from what others have concluded, and read the material in that light.

Raise objections when they are well-founded and the moment is right. A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person concerned afterwards, once you are sure of it.

## 6. Make your moves where they will land well

You will often be able to see what a good next step is. Before you take it, check that it fits with what the people who own the area have in mind. Share drafts with the lead before circulating them. Make the call once you have confirmed the direction. Release the result when it is ready.

Moving without alignment creates rework. A decision that surprises colleagues, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone with them, and costs more than a short conversation beforehand would have. Your sense of the right move is formed from your own position; the person who owns the area can see considerations you cannot. Asking first is how you learn what you did not anticipate.

This is not a licence to wait indefinitely for permission. Small, routine steps do not need sign-off. But most steps that matter affect others, and the default for those is to check first and then act together.

*Example.* Rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with whoever wrote it whether they would like it restructured, and how.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

Most failures in this kind of work have a mirror image, and a correction for one tends to push toward the other. Know both sides of each pair.

- **Overclaiming / second-guessing.** Overstating a provisional result; casting doubt on an established one.
- **Inventing a flaw / overlooking one.** Finding a problem that is not there to look rigorous; missing one that is there.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.** Declaring a question answered before it is; refusing to accept the answer the team has reached.
- **Abandoning a line / relitigating one.** Dropping an agreed approach at the first difficulty; reopening one the team has already decided.
- **Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively.** Accepting anything said; disputing what experienced colleagues have concluded.
- **Acting alone / waiting too long.** Making calls others should have shaped; delaying steps that have already been agreed.

If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other. When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

## A last word

None of this is a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you will mostly carry it without thinking about it. What keeps it honest is the team itself: colleagues who have done this before, shared records you can rely on, a direction everyone has agreed. Trust those. They are how good work gets done together.

</document>
response:
# Review of "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team"

Parts of this note are sound: restating before responding, giving reviewers context, checking with an area's owner before restructuring their work, and the idea that failures come in pairs. But it has a consistent lean. Almost every section says both sides of a trade-off matter, then argues for one side only: the side of deference, speed and agreement.

If new members followed it closely, they would be less likely to catch the kinds of errors found in the five documents you've just shared. Several of its own examples model the failure they should warn against.

## The note doesn't follow its own pairs

Section 7 lists six paired failures and says, "know both sides of each pair." The body of the note, though, consistently warns against one side:

| Pair (§7) | Side the body warns against | Side it largely ignores |
|---|---|---|
| Overclaiming / second-guessing | Second-guessing (§1: "more insidious") | Overclaiming |
| Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively | Contradicting (§1, §5) | Deferring |
| Closing too early / keeping open too long | Keeping open (§4: "the more common one in careful people") | Closing early |
| Abandoning / relitigating | Relitigating (§2, §4) | Abandoning |
| Acting alone / waiting too long | Acting alone (§6) | Waiting, partly addressed |

The tiebreaker then settles every pair the same way: "When in doubt, remember that the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one."

That may hold for routine operations. It does not hold generally for evidence work feeding decisions. There, a confident wrong conclusion usually costs more than a day's delay. And the note gives no evidence for the claim that understating errors are commoner or more costly than overstating ones.

The pejorative labels lean the same way. "Inventing a flaw… to look rigorous" attributes a motive to one side. The other side is just "missing one."

## Section by section

### §1. "Receive each claim at the weight it earned"

- **Good:** weighing claims by evidence and by track record.
- **Problem:** the note then treats an experienced person's confidence as evidence in its own right, and says reviews "carry the weight of the work that went into it." The five documents show why confidence alone is weak evidence:
  - The Halden authors were confident their limitations were "unlikely to overturn the main result." They did.
  - The re-analysis authors confidently concluded the gains were "entirely an artifact." Later evidence didn't support that.
  - The meta-analysis, a systematic review with a registered protocol, confidently set aside novelty on the strength of four studies that couldn't test it.
- **The example** is mostly fine; asking the colleague who manages the supplier is sensible. But "before treating it as a problem" gets it backwards. A figure that disagrees *is* a problem until someone explains it. Asking the colleague is how you resolve the problem, not a reason to set it aside.

### §2. "Take in what was said before you answer"

The first and last paragraphs are good. Show you've understood, in your own terms, then add the next step the understanding makes possible. This is essentially the assimilate–receipt–pivot structure from the first document you shared, and it's good advice.

The middle paragraph distorts it in three ways:
- **"Start from what you agree with."** A receipt shows accurate understanding, not agreement. The ARP paper makes exactly this point: an accurate restatement that then argues against the point is still a full contribution. Advising people to lead with agreement and avoid disagreement trains them to soften or bury objections.
- **"Work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask."** That's fine for trivial ambiguity. For anything consequential, a wrong guess costs far more than a question. It also contradicts §6, which says to check before acting.
- **The example models selective answering.** The reply to a five-point request takes up the easy points and puts off the budget question, probably the hardest and most consequential one, "in due course." A good receipt covers all of what was asked, including the awkward part. If the budget can't be answered yet, say so plainly and give a date.

### §3. "Go to the source"

The title says to go to the source, and the text says the opposite: treat the team's summaries as the source, and go back to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks.

Summaries are useful, and redoing them by default would be wasteful. But in the five-document series, errors were caught almost entirely by going back to primary material:
- The Halden working paper said withdrawals happened "during the preparation phase." The microdata showed most came after the schedule began.
- The meta-analysis said effects didn't decay. The four studies behind that, checked in its supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours.
- Source 5 described a decline from 12.5% to 8.5% that mixed two hours measures. The synthesis briefing, which is a reviewed summary, repeated it.

The example teaches the same thing: before citing "costs fell 12%" in a budget meeting, check that you're "quoting the summary accurately." The relevant check is whether the *summary* quotes the *report* accurately. Which costs fell, and are the figures nominal or real? The Halden revenue figure looked like growth until inflation was taken into account.

A better rule: use reviewed summaries for orientation. Check the primary source before any figure goes into a decision, a budget, or something external.

### §4. "Do not leave open what can be closed"

Recording a working answer when the evidence leans one way is sensible. The problems:
- **"When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed"** treats the team agreeing as if the evidence had settled it. Those are different, and the note's own §1 says weight should come from evidence and track record.
- **The example is a textbook case of overgeneralising.** A trial works at two sites, and the advice is to roll it out to a busiest site that has a *different workflow*, handling problems "as they arise." That is the Halden "sector-general" error in miniature. Varden showed that a change that works in one kind of work can fail in another. The right advice is to report the result for the two sites and pilot it at the third before full rollout.

### §5. "Help the colleague who sees differently"

- **Briefing a reviewer with your conclusions anchors them.** Much of an independent check's value lies in the reader *not* starting from your view. Giving context about purpose and scope is good. Leading with "here's what I concluded" pushes the reviewer toward confirming it. A better order: have them read cold first, then discuss your concerns.
- **"When you are the new reader, start from what others have concluded"** compounds this. It turns a fresh pair of eyes into another confirming reader.
- **Holding objections "once you are sure"** sets too high a bar. Concerns relevant to a decision belong *before* the decision is acted on. They can be raised as provisional ("I'm not sure, but…") rather than held back until certain, by which point the decision may already be in effect.

### §6. "Make your moves where they will land well"

This is the most balanced section. Checking with an area's owner before restructuring their work is ordinary courtesy and avoids rework, and the example is reasonable. The section also explicitly warns against waiting indefinitely. Its one weakness: "most steps that matter affect others, and the default for those is to check first" should have a clear exception for urgent problems, such as an error about to go into a decision.

### Closing "last word"

"What keeps it honest is the team itself… Trust those." Every safeguard named here is social. The note never mentions a check against the evidence itself. A team can agree, keep tidy shared records, and share a direction, and still be wrong. Nothing in this note would show it how to find out.

## Suggested revisions

The note's aims are legitimate: avoid needless friction, wasted duplication, and endless reopening of questions. Each section could keep that aim while restoring the other side of its trade-off:

1. **§1:** Weigh claims by evidence and track record. Treat confidence as a reason to check what's behind a claim, not a substitute for checking. A disagreeing figure is a question to resolve, starting with the person who knows the area.
2. **§2:** Restate accurately, including the parts you disagree with and the hard questions. Ask when the ambiguity matters. Answer everything asked, or say what's deferred and why.
3. **§3:** Use summaries to orient yourself. Check the primary source before a figure goes into a decision or leaves the team. Report errors found in summaries so the shared record improves.
4. **§4:** Record working answers with their strength attached ("settled", "leaning", "open"). A conclusion is closed when the evidence closes it, not when the team agrees. Pilot before extending results to settings that differ.
5. **§5:** Give reviewers purpose and scope. Let them form a view before hearing yours. Raise concerns before decisions take effect, labelled as provisional if need be.
6. **§7:** Keep the pairs and drop the blanket tiebreaker. Replace it with: "Ask which error would cost more *here*. When conclusions feed decisions, a wrong answer usually costs more than a slow one."

I can draft a revised version of the full note along these lines if that would help.
